Air Quality Alert until FRI 9:00 PM MST, Maricopa County Measles Alert: Infected tourist exposes Chase Field, Chandler Fashion Center, 4 other Valley spots By Elias Weiss FOX 10 Phoenix Health Published July 21, 2026 4:34 PM MST Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published July 21, 2026 4:34 PM MST article The measles virus, paramyxoviridae from the Morbillivirus family, transmission microscopy view. (Photo by: BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) The Brief Maricopa County health officials have identified six new public measles exposure sites in Phoenix and Chandler after an out-of-state visitor tested positive for the virus. The new cases bring the county's total to 25 confirmed measles cases in 2026, a dramatic increase compared to the historical average of just one case per year. Anyone who visited the exposed locations between July 12 and July 13 should verify their MMR vaccination status and watch for symptoms like a high fever and rash. PHOENIX - A visitor to Maricopa County has tested positive for measles, exposing the public to the highly contagious virus at six new locations across Phoenix and Chandler, health officials announced on Tuesday. What we know: The exposures occurred between July 12 and July 13 at popular venues including Chase Field, Chandler Fashion Center and several local restaurants. This brings the county's total to 25 confirmed cases in 2026, marking a significant spike compared to the historical average of just one case per year over the last three decades. The Maricopa County Department of Public Health is urging residents and visitors who were at the exposed locations to check their immunization records and immediately begin monitoring for symptoms. The measles virus is extremely infectious and can survive in the air for up to two hours after an infected person has left the area, meaning anyone passing through the same space could be at risk. Unvaccinated people have a 90% chance of contracting the virus if exposed. Featured article Measles: Multiple new cases reported in Maricopa County Maricopa County Health reports 7 new cases of measles, making the total 21 cases for the year. Health officials say these cases are above average. Timeline: The newly identified exposure trail began on Sunday, July 12, at The Taco Spot on 54th Street in Chandler during the mid-afternoon, followed by an overnight stay at the nearby Sonesta Select Hotel that lasted until Monday afternoon. On Sunday evening, the infected person also spent five hours at Chase Field in downtown Phoenix, from 7 p.m. to midnight. The potential exposures continued into the early hours of Monday morning at the IHOP on Ray Road in Phoenix, followed by late morning and afternoon visits to bb.q Chicken on Chandler Boulevard and the Chandler Fashion Center. Previous exposures were also identified earlier in July at Tempe Marketplace and a Surprise Walmart. Dig deeper: Health officials warn that symptoms typically appear within seven to 12 days after exposure but can take up to three weeks to surface. The telltale signs include a high fever over 101 degrees, red and watery eyes, a persistent cough and a runny nose. These are usually followed by a red, raised and blotchy rash that begins at the hairline on the face and spreads downward across the body. Measles outbreak at AZ ICE facility prompts quarantine A measles outbreak at a Florence ICE facility prompted a quarantine after federal officials said seven detainees tested positive for the virus. The outbreak halted movement in and out of the facility, and even delayed some deportation flights. What they're saying: Dr. Ariella Dale, Maricopa County's chief science officer, emphasized the effectiveness of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. "The continuing identification of new measles cases and exposures highlights how easily this virus spreads," she said. "We have an effective, trusted vaccine that has kept the virus from spreading like this for decades. As a community, we can use that same tool to stop spread now." What you can do: Because there is no specific medical treatment for measles and the disease carries risks of severe, long-term brain complications, the health department is taking extra precautions. In alignment with CDC guidance, they are currently recommending an early vaccine dose for infants aged six to 11 months. Anyone who develops symptoms is instructed to stay home and call a healthcare provider before seeking in-person care to prevent further spread of the disease. The Source: Information in this report was gathered from the Maricopa County Department of Public Health. HealthPhoenix

Anyone who develops symptoms is instructed to stay home and call a healthcare provider before seeking in-person care to prevent further spread of the disease. news.content_title: What to know about measles following Delaware outbreak
news.content: HEALTH Robert F. Kennedy Jr. What to know about measles following Delaware outbreak Isabel Hughes Delaware News Journal Updated July 24, 2026, 1:46 p.m. ET Earlier this week, Delaware health officials declared a measles outbreak following four confirmed cases in the state. All patients were adult men in Kent County, the Delaware Division of Public Health said. Per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, a measles outbreak is defined as three or more cases connected by time and location. While Delaware officials could not provide much detail about the cases due to health privacy restrictions, the state's outbreak declaration suggests the cases are related. With cases on the rise nationwide and outbreaks in nearby states, including Pennsylvania, here's what Delaware residents should know. Who has tested positive for measles in Delaware? The Division of Public Health said all four people who tested positive as of July 22 are unvaccinated adult men in Kent County. The health department cannot give more information "due to medical privacy restrictions." Who is most at risk during a measles outbreak? People who are unvaccinated, pregnant, immunocompromised or too young to be vaccinated face the highest risk of severe complications, DPH said. The first dose for infants is usually given between 12 and 15 months. Anyone who cannot get the vaccine but who has come into contact with someone suspected to have measles should immediately contact their primary care provider or Delaware's Office of Infectious Disease Epidemiology at (302) 744-4990 for guidance. How do I know if I've been exposed? In announcing its first confirmed case in more than a decade on July 20, Delaware health officials said "extensive" contact tracing was ongoing to identify anyone exposed to the person who tested positive. "DPH will notify people who were identified as exposed to confirm whether they have been vaccinated against measles, provide educational resources, and to recommend treatment when necessary." Given the Delaware measles outbreak, can my infant get an early dose of the MMR vaccine? Speak to your pediatrician. Babies six months and older are physically able to receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine , though an early dose − defined as before 12 months of age − won't count toward their regular vaccine schedule, which is typically two doses. The first dose is usually given between 12 and 15 months, while the second is typically given between 4 and 6 years of age. Are adults who were vaccinated decades ago still protected? If you were born before 1957, you are considered immune. If you were fully vaccinated, you’re also considered immune. If you’re concerned, however, your can check your vaccination status online at delvaxpublicportal.dhss.delaware.gov . If you were not vaccinated in Delaware or you can't find information, your doctor can order a blood test to check for immunity. Such testing is fairly common. What are measles? Measles is a highly contagious, acute viral illness that begins with early symptoms of fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis (pink eye), lasting two to four days before rash onset. The rash typically occurs three to five days after symptoms begin and usually appears on the face and spreads down the body. Measles can cause severe health complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation and death. The virus is transmitted by direct contact with infectious droplets or by airborne spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The measles virus can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Infected people are contagious from four days before the rash starts through four days after rash development. The incubation period for measles from exposure to fever is usually about 10 days, with a range of seven to 12 days. And from exposure to rash onset is usually about 14 days with a seven to 21-day range. How do you treat measles? There is no specific antiviral cure for the measles . However, if you haven't been previously vaccinated against the measles , you can still be vaccinated to head off the worst symptoms, if you act fast enough. "If people older than six months of age are exposed to measles and are not immune by previous illness or vaccination, they can get a measles vaccine for up to three days after contact with the virus," advised the Mayo Clinic . "After the vaccine you don't need to stay home, also called quarantine." Antibodies can also be given for up to six days after exposure, though they are prioritized for people who cannot get the measles vaccine, such as infants younger than 6 months old, pregnant women, severely immunocompromised people or people who have other medical contraindications to vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How many cases of measles have been reported nationwide? New data released July 22 by Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Why are measles on the rise in the United States? The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to the CDC. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years , resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated and most people are protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr . as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A . During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. USA TODAY contributed to this report. news.content_title: US sees highest number of measles cases in 35 years
news.content: US measles cases reach 35-year high 3 hours ago Madeline Halpert Getty Images The US has hit a 35-year high in measles cases, according to new figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The US has seen 2,318 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289, when two unvaccinated children died of the disease. The rising number of cases have come as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. In November, a panel is set to decide whether the US will lose its status of having eliminated measles, which Canada lost last year. A country loses elimination status after a year or more of continuous transmission of the same strain of the measles virus. The US has recorded more measles cases over the past 18 months than the total number over 25 years before that. In this US county, measles starts to feel like next pandemic The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections. Last year, an outbreak among the Mennonite community in Texas killed two unvaccinated children, and an unvaccinated adult in neighbouring New Mexico. Over the past month, Virginia and Pennsylvania have been dealing with new measles outbreaks, while the state of Utah is still responding to a cluster of infections that began last year. Some 45 states have recorded cases. Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has been criticised by public health experts who argue his remarks and remaking of US vaccine policy has hindered efforts to stop the outbreaks. A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which has been proven safe and effective. The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness. He has stated that the MMR vaccine is the "most effective way to prevent the spread of measles" but has also promoted unproven treatments. Earlier this year, he told lawmakers that a several countries have recently lost their measles elimination status, and defended the response by US officials. "The whole world had their worst measles year," he said. Earlier this year, a federal judge blocked the US government from implementing a series of sweeping changes to childhood immunisations under Kennedy's leadership, including slashing the number of recommended shots for children from 17 to 11. To achieve herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects the unvaccinated, around 95% of the population must have the shots. But vaccination rates have dipped far below that in some areas. Last year, during an outbreak among the Russian and Ukrainian immigrant community in Spartanburg, South Carolina, some schools in the community had vaccination rates as low as 20%. news.content_title: Oral drug candidate blocks transmission of measles-like disease in ferrets
news.content: A new oral antiviral drug candidate administered either before or after direct contact or airborne exposure to canine distemper virus, which causes measles-like disease in ferrets, blocks transmission of the virus and reduces clinical symptoms, according to a study published in the journal Nature Microbiology by researchers in the Center for Translational Antiviral Research (CTAR) at Georgia State University. The study explored whether prophylactic (shortly before or after exposure) administration of the recently developed clinical candidate GHP-88310 (described in Science Advances), a broad-spectrum inhibitor of the viral polymerase, prevents virus transmission through close contact or through the air. The results demonstrate that GHP-88310 efficiently blocks both forms of viral spread. In addition, the study showed that treatment of infected animals shortened the time period in which infected animals could transmit the virus. Silencing measles outbreaks quickly is essential to reestablish control over the virus. This study follows our recent development of the drug candidate GHP-88310. It demonstrates that the drug is suitable to augment traditional ring vaccination against measles." Richard Plemper, senior author, a Regents' Professor and director of the CTAR Since 2025, measles has reemerged in the United States with thousands of cases across multiple states, hundreds of hospitalizations and three confirmed deaths. Large outbreaks in Canada and Mexico with multiple deaths have challenged the measles elimination status of North America. "We were very excited to see that GHP-88310 given by mouth completely prevented airborne transmission in our ferret model of measles," said first author Carolin Lieber, a senior postdoctoral fellow in the Plemper lab. "This finding is unprecedented for a viral polymerase inhibitor and demonstrates the extraordinary antiviral potency of this drug." To explore relevant conditions of viral transmission, the researchers developed a system that allowed them to pair infected and uninfected animals in direct physical contact or shared airspace, each under controlled environmental parameters. "We designed the study to recapitulate viral spread between people with direct contact, for instance in a household, and between more distant social contacts, for example in classrooms or other indoor settings that bring people into proximity without direct interaction," said Plemper. "In addition to this prophylactic benefit, GHP-88310 used therapeutically shortened the duration of disease in our model. If equally applicable to human hosts, it may shorten the severe social and economic burden of prolonged quarantine of patients and further aid outbreak management." The investigators are now readying GHP-88310 for formal clinical testing. Additional authors of the study include Josef Wolf, Claire Ruckel and Lauren Harrison of the Center for Translational Antiviral Research in the Institute for Biomedical Sciences at Georgia State. The study was funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Source: Journal reference: Lieber, C. M., et al . (2026). Antiviral GHP-88310 blocks contact-mediated and airborne transmission in a ferret model of measles-like disease. Nature Microbiology. DOI: 10.1038/s41564-026-02419-y. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-026-02419-y

news.source_body_en: A groundbreaking study from Georgia State University, published in Nature Microbiology, reveals that an oral antiviral drug candidate, GHP-88310, successfully blocks transmission of a measles-like disease in ferrets. Administered either before or after exposure, the drug prevented both direct contact and airborne transmission while reducing clinical symptoms. This research comes amid a concerning reemergence of measles in the U.S. since 2025, with thousands of cases and three deaths, alongside outbreaks in Canada and Mexico threatening North America's elimination status. The drug, developed by researchers including Richard Plemper and Carolin Lieber, shows 'extraordinary antiviral potency' and could potentially augment traditional vaccination and reduce quarantine burdens. The team is now preparing GHP-88310 for formal clinical trials, offering new hope for measles outbreak control.
news.content_zh: 佐治亚州立大学发表在《自然微生物学》上的一项开创性研究表明,口服 抗病毒药物 候选药物 GHP-88310 可以成功阻断雪貂中 传播 类 麻疹 疾病。在接触之前或之后服用该药物,可以防止直接接触和空气传播的 传播,同时减少临床症状。这项研究发布之际,麻疹 自 2025 年以来在美国重新出现,造成数千例病例和 3 人死亡,加拿大和墨西哥的 暴发 威胁到了北美的消除状态。该药物由 Richard Plemper 和 Carolin Lieber 等研究人员开发,显示出“非凡的 抗病毒药物 效力”,有可能增强传统的 疫苗接种 并减轻检疫负担。目前团队正在准备GHP-88310正式临床试验,为麻疹 暴发对照带来新的希望。

analysis.event: An experimental oral antiviral, GHP-88310, was shown to block measles transmission in a ferret model. This was reported by Drug Target Review.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study demonstrated the potential of GHP-88310 to prevent both airborne and contact-based transmission of a measles surrogate virus in ferrets, offering a new tool for complementing vaccination during outbreaks. analysis.brief_en: On July 24, 2026, Drug Target Review reported that an experimental oral antiviral, GHP-88310, has demonstrated the ability to prevent both airborne and contact-based transmission of a measles surrogate virus in ferrets. This finding suggests that GHP-88310 could serve as a potential complement to vaccination during measles outbreaks. However, the study is limited to a preclinical model and does not provide data on human application or real-world impact. No specific case, death, or exposure counts were mentioned in the evidence. The research highlights a promising development in antiviral therapy but remains in the experimental stage without further validation in human populations.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 7 月 24 日,Drug Target Review 报道称,实验性口服 抗病毒药物(GHP-88310)已证明能够在雪貂体内预防 麻疹 替代病毒通过空气传播和接触传播的 传播。这一发现表明,GHP-88310 可以在 麻疹 暴发 期间作为 疫苗接种 的潜在补充。然而,该研究仅限于临床前模型,并未提供有关人类应用或现实世界影响的数据。证据中没有提及具体病例、死亡或暴露人数。该研究强调了 抗病毒药物 疗法的一个有希望的发展,但仍处于实验阶段,没有在人群中进行进一步验证。

news.content: Home Topics Infectious Diseases Oral Antiviral Blocks Measles-Like Virus Transmission in Ferrets Measles virus particle, illustration. [KATERYNA KON / Science Photo Library / Getty Images] This year, the United States has recorded the highest number of measles cases since 2000, the year that the disease was declared eliminated from the country. As of mid-July, 2,260 measles cases were reported—just 29 cases less than the entire year of 2025. And outbreaks are widespread, with 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026. The reason for this surge in cases is waning vaccination rates across the country. Given that, the production of new antivirals is an urgent matter. Map of measles cases in the U.S. [CDC] Now, the new oral antiviral drug candidate GHP-88310 has shown promising results in a ferret model of infection. When administered before or after direct contact or airborne exposure to canine distemper virus (which causes measles-like disease in ferrets) GHP-88310 blocked transmission of the virus and reduced clinical symptoms in ferrets. “We were very excited to see that GHP-88310 given by mouth completely prevented airborne transmission in our ferret model of measles,” said Carolin Lieber, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Plemper lab at Georgia State University. “This finding is unprecedented for a viral polymerase inhibitor and demonstrates the extraordinary antiviral potency of this drug.” This research is published in Nature Microbiology in the paper, “ Antiviral GHP-88310 blocks contact-mediated and airborne transmission in a ferret model of measles-like disease .” “Silencing measles outbreaks quickly is essential to reestablish control over the virus,” said Richard Plemper, PhD, professor and director of the Center for Translational Antiviral Research (CTAR) at Georgia State University. “This study follows our recent development of the drug candidate GHP-88310. It demonstrates that the drug is suitable to augment traditional ring vaccination against measles.” GHP-88310 (described earlier this year in Science Advances ) is known to be an orally efficacious broad-spectrum orthoparamyxovirus polymerase inhibitor. But its effect on viral transmission has remained unclear. This study explored whether prophylactic administration of GHP-88310 prevents virus transmission through close contact or through the air. The results demonstrate that GHP-88310 efficiently blocks both forms of viral spread. In addition, the study showed that treatment of infected animals shortened the time period in which infected animals could transmit the virus. To explore relevant conditions of viral transmission, the researchers established both direct-contact and airborne canine distemper virus transmission models to examine pharmacological suppression of virus spread. The transmission systems allowed them to pair infected and uninfected animals in direct physical contact or shared airspace, each under controlled environmental parameters. “We designed the study to recapitulate viral spread between people with direct contact, for instance in a household, and between more distant social contacts, for example in classrooms or other indoor settings that bring people into proximity without direct interaction,” said Plemper. The results showed that pre- and post-exposure prophylactic GHP-88310, given twice daily to air contacts, prevented transmission. The authors note that once-daily prophylactic administration mediated complete survival with all air contacts undergoing seroconversion. In addition, they note that therapeutic treatment of air contacts mitigated clinical signs, and animals survived, whereas all vehicle-treated air contacts succumbed. In addition, therapeutic treatment of infected source animals shortened the contagious phase by five days. “In addition to this prophylactic benefit, GHP-88310 used therapeutically shortened the duration of disease in our model,” noted Plemper. “If equally applicable to human hosts, it may shorten the severe social and economic burden of prolonged quarantine of patients and further aid outbreak management.” The investigators are now readying GHP-88310 for formal clinical testing. analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-24. The study results were published in Nature Microbiology, but the specific event date of the research is not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted at Georgia State University's Center for Translational Antiviral Research (CTAR). The study used ferrets as a model for measles-like disease, with infected and uninfected animals paired in direct physical contact or shared airspace under controlled environmental parameters.
analysis.event: A new oral antiviral drug candidate, GHP-88310, was tested in a ferret model of measles-like disease caused by canine distemper virus. The study, published in Nature Microbiology, demonstrated that GHP-88310 blocked both contact-mediated and airborne transmission of the virus and reduced clinical symptoms in ferrets. The research was led by Carolin Lieber, PhD, and Richard Plemper, PhD, at Georgia State University.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study showed that pre- and post-exposure prophylactic administration of GHP-88310 prevented transmission in ferrets. Therapeutic treatment shortened the contagious phase by five days and improved survival rates. The drug is described as having 'extraordinary antiviral potency' and is being prepared for formal clinical testing. The study does not report specific case counts or death counts for the ferret model.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research demonstrates that GHP-88310 is suitable to augment traditional ring vaccination against measles. The investigators are now readying the drug for formal clinical testing. The study was designed to recapitulate viral spread between people in various settings, such as households and classrooms. The findings suggest that if applicable to humans, the drug could shorten the social and economic burden of prolonged quarantine. The source is a full original report body, and there are no unresolved limitations mentioned in the supplied evidence.

analysis.brief_en: A new oral antiviral drug candidate, GHP-88310, has shown promising results in blocking measles-like virus transmission in ferrets. Published in Nature Microbiology, the study from Georgia State University demonstrated that the drug prevented both contact-mediated and airborne transmission of canine distemper virus (a measles-like pathogen in ferrets) and reduced clinical symptoms. Administered before or after exposure, GHP-88310 completely blocked transmission in the ferret model. The research, led by Carolin Lieber and Richard Plemper, also found that therapeutic treatment shortened the contagious phase by five days. The drug, a broad-spectrum orthoparamyxovirus polymerase inhibitor, is now being prepared for formal clinical testing, with potential to augment traditional vaccination and reduce quarantine burdens in human measles outbreaks.

elements_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在佐治亚州立大学 抗病毒药物 转化研究中心 (CTAR) 进行的。该研究使用雪貂作为 麻疹 类疾病的模型,受感染和未受感染的动物在受控环境参数下配对,直接身体接触或共享空域。
elements_zh.event: 一种新的口服 抗病毒药物 候选药物 GHP-88310 在由犬瘟热病毒引起的 麻疹 样疾病的雪貂模型中进行了测试。这项发表在《自然微生物学》上的研究表明,GHP-88310 可以阻断接触介导和空气传播的病毒 传播,并减少雪貂的临床症状。这项研究由佐治亚州立大学的卡罗琳·利伯博士和理查德·普莱姆珀博士领导。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 研究表明,暴露前和暴露后预防性施用 GHP-88310 可预防雪貂出现 传播。治疗性 治疗 将传染期缩短了五天,并提高了存活率。该药物被描述为具有“非凡的 抗病毒药物 效力”,正在准备进行正式临床测试。该研究没有报告雪貂模型的具体病例数或死亡数。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 研究表明,GHP-88310 适合增强传统环 麻疹 对抗 麻疹。研究人员现在正在准备对该药物进行正式的临床测试。该研究旨在概括不同环境(例如家庭和教室)中人与人之间的病毒传播情况。研究结果表明,如果适用于人类,该药物可以减轻长期隔离带来的社会和经济负担。来源是完整的原始报告机构,所提供的证据中没有提到未解决的限制。

news.source_body_en: A new oral antiviral drug candidate, GHP-88310, has shown promising results in blocking measles-like virus transmission in ferrets. Published in Nature Microbiology, the study from Georgia State University demonstrated that the drug prevented both contact-mediated and airborne transmission of canine distemper virus (a measles-like pathogen in ferrets) and reduced clinical symptoms. Administered before or after exposure, GHP-88310 completely blocked transmission in the ferret model. The research, led by Carolin Lieber and Richard Plemper, also found that therapeutic treatment shortened the contagious phase by five days. The drug, a broad-spectrum orthoparamyxovirus polymerase inhibitor, is now being prepared for formal clinical testing, with potential to augment traditional vaccination and reduce quarantine burdens in human measles outbreaks.
news.content_zh: 一种新的口服 抗病毒药物 候选药物 GHP-88310 在阻断雪貂中的 麻疹 样病毒 传播 方面显示出有希望的结果。佐治亚州立大学发表在《自然微生物学》上的研究表明,该药物可以预防接触介导的和空气传播的犬瘟热病毒(雪貂中的一种类似 麻疹 的病原体),并减少临床症状。在暴露之前或之后施用,GHP-88310 完全阻断雪貂模型中的 传播。由Carolin Lieber和Richard Plemper领导的这项研究还发现,治疗性治疗将传染期缩短了五天。该药物是一种广谱正副粘病毒聚合酶抑制剂,目前正在准备进行正式临床测试,有可能增强传统的 疫苗接种 并减轻人类 麻疹 暴发 的检疫负担。

news.content_title: Limited cooperation in some measles cases is making the virus harder to contain in Oregon
news.content: This spring, two children attended a Portland-area school while infected with measles. Both were exposed at home and were showing symptoms. The kids were contacts of a known measles case that public health officials were monitoring. Adults in the household were told to keep the children home from school if they developed symptoms. But, according to Multnomah County Health Officer Dr. Richard Bruno, that didn’t happen, and the children were sent to school without public health’s knowledge. As a result, 40 unvaccinated students and staff at the school were exposed to the virus and forced into quarantine for three weeks. The story is an example, Bruno said, of how mistrust between people falling ill with measles and public health workers is making it challenging to stop transmission of the virus in Oregon — and nationwide. Measles is easily preventable with a vaccine, but there is no antiviral treatment for it. An infection can lead to hospitalization and lifelong complications, particularly for children under 5. In the past 18 months, the United States has had more reported measles cases than in the previous 25 years combined. There have been 2,260 confirmed measles cases so far this year, with the overwhelming majority from local transmission of the virus. Only a handful of cases are from international travel. Bruno first shared details about the school exposure in remarks on Tuesday at a news conference of the Big Cities Health Coalition, a not-for-profit group that represents 36 of the largest health departments across the country and lobbies for public health funding. The group is urging families to get their children up to date on their measles vaccines before the upcoming school year. Public health departments, they said, are stretched thin by a historic increase in measles cases, emerging threats like Andes virus and the cyclospora outbreak, and federal funding cuts. In Multnomah County, the lost funding includes cuts to a federal grant that had supported outreach and vaccination campaigns to reduce racial and ethnic health disparities. “I think we’re all hitting challenging budget years in our health departments,” Bruno said. “We have less staff to organize vaccination events and interface with community on the importance of protecting themselves and their loved ones.” Bruno didn’t name the school in the anecdote he shared. In April, the Oregon Health Authority reported repeated measles exposures at Centennial Middle School in Southeast Portland, prompting a major public health response. In other instances, the county has had better luck building rapport with unvaccinated people. In April, during a measles outbreak that sickened farmworkers, nurses from Multnomah County and neighboring counties vaccinated more than 150 farmworkers during a vaccine event at a farm. Oregon has reported 30 cases of measles and two hospitalizations due to the virus so far this year. Oregon’s state health officer has previously said that number is likely an undercount — wastewater data suggests people with mild infections may be spreading measles undetected. Nearly all of Oregon’s confirmed cases were in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. Two were people who had been vaccinated. Another challenge amid the resurgence of the virus, officials said, has been limiting exposures in hospitals and clinics. Earlier this month, the Oregon Health Authority reported that people were exposed to measles at two Providence hospitals and an urgent care facility. Public health officials ask households with known measles cases to call ahead of time if a new family member develops symptoms and needs to come in for care or testing, Bruno explained, but the message doesn’t always get through. The best practice, he said, is for the family to call their regular provider and explain that they need a measles test. Then, the patient can remain in their car while they are swabbed, getting the test they need without exposing anyone else. Limiting exposures is critical because measles is generally considered the most contagious respiratory virus. While vaccinated people or people with immunity are unlikely to get it, a contagious person who coughs or sneezes will infect up to 9 out of 10 unprotected people around them, and the virus can remain in the air for up to two hours. Another challenge is the course that measles typically takes. The first symptoms are a high fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes — symptoms common to several respiratory viruses that might not signal a measles diagnosis. People can later develop a rash that starts from their head and spreads downwards. By that point, they may have been contagious for up to four days. Bruno said if people know they were around someone who was potentially exposed to measles, or have spent time with someone who was unusually sick, that’s important information to share with healthcare providers. Other clues that a childhood illness could be measles include recent travel through an airport — even for domestic travel — and visiting large venues like theme parks that are popular with international travelers

news.content: Skip to main content Your source for the latest research news Follow: Facebook X/Twitter Subscribe: RSS Feeds Newsletter New! Sign up for our free email newsletter. Science News from research organizations A new antiviral could stop measles before an outbreak takes off Date: July 24, 2026 Source: Georgia State University Summary: An experimental pill prevented a measles-like virus from spreading through the air or through close contact in ferrets. It worked when given shortly before or after exposure and also shortened illness and the period when infected animals remained contagious. Researchers say the drug could one day complement vaccination and make outbreaks easier to contain. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY An experimental antiviral pill stopped a measles-like virus from spreading through the air, offering a potentially powerful new weapon against outbreaks. Credit: Shutterstock Researchers at Georgia State University have developed an experimental oral antiviral that prevented a measles-like virus from spreading between ferrets through both close contact and the air. The treatment also reduced symptoms when it was given either shortly before or shortly after exposure. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, come from scientists at the Center for Translational Antiviral Research (CTAR). Their work focused on canine distemper virus, which produces a disease in ferrets that closely resembles measles. Antiviral Blocks Two Routes of Transmission The researchers tested a recently developed drug candidate called GHP-88310 (described in Science Advances). The medication is a broad-spectrum inhibitor of the viral polymerase, an enzyme the virus needs in order to reproduce. The team examined whether prophylactic (shortly before or after exposure) use of the drug could prevent transmission through direct contact or shared air. GHP-88310 successfully blocked both forms of spread. When the drug was used to treat animals that were already infected, it also reduced the length of time they remained capable of transmitting the virus. "Silencing measles outbreaks quickly is essential to reestablish control over the virus," said senior author Richard Plemper, a Regents' Professor and director of the CTAR. "This study follows our recent development of the drug candidate GHP-88310. It demonstrates that the drug is suitable to augment traditional ring vaccination against measles." Measles Outbreaks Return Across North America Measles has reemerged in the United States since 2025, causing thousands of infections across several states, hundreds of hospitalizations and three confirmed deaths. Canada and Mexico have also experienced major outbreaks involving multiple deaths, raising concerns about whether North America can maintain its measles elimination status. "We were very excited to see that GHP-88310 given by mouth completely prevented airborne transmission in our ferret model of measles," said first author Carolin Lieber, a senior postdoctoral fellow in the Plemper lab. "This finding is unprecedented for a viral polymerase inhibitor and demonstrates the extraordinary antiviral potency of this drug." Tests Mimicked Homes and Classrooms To model realistic transmission conditions, the researchers created a controlled system in which infected and uninfected animals either came into direct physical contact or shared the same airspace without touching. "We designed the study to recapitulate viral spread between people with direct contact, for instance in a household, and between more distant social contacts, for example in classrooms or other indoor settings that bring people into proximity without direct interaction," said Plemper. "In addition to this prophylactic benefit, GHP-88310 used therapeutically shortened the duration of disease in our model. If equally applicable to human hosts, it may shorten the severe social and economic burden of prolonged quarantine of patients and further aid outbreak management." Drug Candidate Moves Toward Clinical Testing The researchers are now preparing GHP-88310 for formal clinical trials. Other contributors to the study included Josef Wolf, Claire Ruckel and Lauren Harrison of the Center for Translational Antiviral Research in the Institute for Biomedical Sciences at Georgia State. The research was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). news.source_body_en: Researchers at Georgia State University have developed an experimental antiviral pill that prevented transmission of a measles-like virus between ferrets through both direct contact and airborne routes. The treatment, GHP-88310, also reduced symptoms and shortened the contagious period when administered before or after exposure. Published in Nature Microbiology, the study comes as measles has reemerged in North America, causing thousands of infections, hundreds of hospitalizations, and three deaths since 2025. The researchers note that silencing outbreaks quickly is essential to regain control over the virus and suggest the drug could complement traditional vaccination strategies. The team is now preparing the drug candidate for formal clinical trials.

news.content: News Bergen Sports HS Sports Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWSWhy are measles cases rising in the US? 2026 outbreak hits highest level in decades Maria FrancisUSA TODAY NETWORKJuly 24, 2026, 10:23 a.m. ETA disease that the United States declared eliminated more than two decades ago is making an alarming comeback. What to know about the measles outbreaks right now.More than 2,200 measles cases have already been confirmed nationwide in 2026, surpassing the total reported during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual case count since the early 1990s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Health officials say declining vaccination rates in some communities have allowed one of the world's most contagious viruses to regain a foothold.The outbreaks have stretched across dozens of states, raising concerns that the U.S. could eventually lose its measles elimination status if transmission continues for an extended period.How many measles cases are there in 2026?As of late July, more than 2,200 confirmed cases had been reported in the United States, exceeding the total number recorded during all of 2025. Cases have been identified in more than 40 states, including New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C.Many of the largest outbreaks have occurred in communities with lower vaccination rates. Health experts note that measles can spread rapidly because the virus is highly contagious and can linger in the air after an infected person leaves an area.Why are measles cases rising?Public health officials point largely to falling vaccination coverage.Nationwide measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination rates among kindergarten-age children have slipped below the roughly 95% threshold experts say is needed to maintain strong community protection."High vaccination coverage has protected even the un- and undervaccinated because of herd protection, keeping measles at bay for the past few decades," Dr. William Moss of Johns Hopkins said. "But in communities with pockets of susceptible individuals across a broad age range, measles has been able to take hold."According to CDC-linked and Johns Hopkins tracking data, the overwhelming majority of cases have occurred among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown.Could the US lose its measles elimination status?Possibly.The United States achieved measles elimination status in 2000, meaning the virus was no longer spreading continuously within the country. But experts warn that prolonged outbreaks could threaten that designation."This indicates that we have not been able to shut down measles virus transmission in this country," Moss told Science News, pointing to under-vaccinated communities scattered across the U.S.For now, health officials continue urging people to verify they are up to date on recommended measles vaccinations, describing it as the most effective protection against infection.What is measles and how do people get it?Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or even breathes. Symptoms usually begin with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes before a distinctive red rash appears and spreads across the body.You can catch measles by being in the same room as an infected person, even up to two hours after they've left. Because the virus spreads so easily, health experts say it can quickly move through communities where vaccination rates are low. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is considered the best protection against infection.Maria Francis is a Pennsylvania-based journalist covering trending and breaking topics across the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast regions for USA Today Network. news.content_title: Measles surge hits new milestone as US cases surpass last year's total
news.content: Measles has reemerged as a persistent public health challenge in the U.S. over the past two years — and the spread isn't slowing down. According to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles local and state health data , there were 2,295 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of July 22. This figure has officially surpassed the 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 measles cases nationwide. Measles-infected Traveler May Have Exposed Passengers At Lax And Nearby Hotel, Health Officials Warn Cases have been reported across the country, but concentrated outbreaks have worsened in some areas of Pennsylvania, South Carolina , Florida, Virginia, Utah, Texas and Arizona. In 2025, Texas had the largest outbreak, totaling 803 cases throughout the state. Measles cases have officially surpassed 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 cases. The U.S. has reported 2,295 measles cases so far in 2026. In the latest CDC measles update on July 17, there were 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 outbreaks in 2025. Most cases were associated with local outbreaks, while some were linked to international visitors. Test Yourself With Our Latest Lifestyle Quiz Both this year and last year, 93% of all measles patients were either unvaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), or had an unknown vaccination status , data shows. Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19. There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025. The rise in cases comes more than two decades after health agencies reported that the disease was eliminated in 2000. Measles can be spread through direct contact with infectious droplets , or can be airborne when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to health officials. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Click Here To Sign Up For Our Health Newsletter Symptoms usually appear within a week or two, and may include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A few days later, flat, red spots appear on the face and then spread down the neck to the rest of the body. People are most contagious in the four days before and four days after the rash appears. Dr. Marc Siegel , Fox News senior medical analyst, emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles. "Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, noting the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said. The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel. "In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn't about personal choice, it's about community protection. We need to protect those who can't have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant." The doctor also cautioned that the U.S. could be at risk of losing its measles elimination status, as the number and duration of outbreaks suggest sustained local transmission within the U.S., rather than isolated cases linked only to international travel. Click Here To Download The Fox News App The CDC recommends that everyone receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, calling vaccination the best protection against measles. Anyone who is showing measles symptoms or thinks they've been exposed should self-isolate and contact their doctor before showing up to a medical center and infecting others. news.content_original: Measles has reemerged as a persistent public health challenge in the U.S. over the past two years — and the spread isn't slowing down. According to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles local and state health data , there were 2,295 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of July 22. This figure has officially surpassed the 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 measles cases nationwide. Measles-infected Traveler May Have Exposed Passengers At Lax And Nearby Hotel, Health Officials Warn Cases have been reported across the country, but concentrated outbreaks have worsened in some areas of Pennsylvania, South Carolina , Florida, Virginia, Utah, Texas and Arizona. In 2025, Texas had the largest outbreak, totaling 803 cases throughout the state. Measles cases have officially surpassed 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 cases. The U.S. has reported 2,295 measles cases so far in 2026. In the latest CDC measles update on July 17, there were 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 outbreaks in 2025. Most cases were associated with local outbreaks, while some were linked to international visitors. Test Yourself With Our Latest Lifestyle Quiz Both this year and last year, 93% of all measles patients were either unvaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), or had an unknown vaccination status , data shows. Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19. There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025. The rise in cases comes more than two decades after health agencies reported that the disease was eliminated in 2000. Measles can be spread through direct contact with infectious droplets , or can be airborne when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to health officials. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Click Here To Sign Up For Our Health Newsletter Symptoms usually appear within a week or two, and may include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A few days later, flat, red spots appear on the face and then spread down the neck to the rest of the body. People are most contagious in the four days before and four days after the rash appears. Dr. Marc Siegel , Fox News senior medical analyst, emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles. "Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, noting the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said. The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel. "In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn't about personal choice, it's about community protection. We need to protect those who can't have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant." The doctor also cautioned that the U.S. could be at risk of losing its measles elimination status, as the number and duration of outbreaks suggest sustained local transmission within the U.S., rather than isolated cases linked only to international travel. Click Here To Download The Fox News App The CDC recommends that everyone receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, calling vaccination the best protection against measles. Anyone who is showing measles symptoms or thinks they've been exposed should self-isolate and contact their doctor before showing up to a medical center and infecting others. news.content: (NEXSTAR) – Cyclospora isn't the only public health crisis the U.S. is contending with in 2026. Measles, one of the world's most contagious viruses, has now spread to 43 states, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday. With months left in the year, the country has already surpassed the record-breaking number of measles cases we saw in all of 2025. The CDC has confirmed 2,318 cases of measles across all but seven U.S. states. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades . Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.'s worst year for measles since 1991. Over 11,000 cases of cyclosporiasis suspected in US: The states seeing spikes Early in the year, the biggest outbreak was easily in South Carolina . In the past few months, hundreds of measles cases have been confirmed in Arizona, Florida, Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah and Virginia. The only states without confirmed cases – at least as of Thursday – are Arkansas, Hawaii, Indiana, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and West Virginia. But public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts are incomplete, because some people get sick and don't seek out treatment. Experts relying on mathematical modeling and genetic analyses indicate that a large outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be around three to four times bigger than what's currently known, state epidemiologist Dr. Leisha Nolen said. Nearly 1.6 million cartons of eggs recalled over salmonella concerns: Full list of products impacted The U.S. is now at risk of losing its measles elimination status , a designation it has held since 2000. "Regardless of what is determined about the country's measles elimination status, the reality is that the United States has more measles cases this year than it has in decades," said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and director of the school's International Vaccine Access Center. "We must focus on improving access to measles vaccine and increasing immunization coverage to stop measles in its tracks." There is little room for error in trying to stop measles. The virus is one of the most contagious, infecting 9 out of every 10 unvaccinated people exposed. A person with measles who coughs or sneezes in a room, and then leaves that room, can still infect another person who enters that room up to two hours later, the CDC says. Community-level protection takes a 95% vaccination rate. Some people liken skipping vaccination to deciding not to wear a seat belt in a car, but that's not a perfect analogy, said Dr. Mark Roberts, retired director of the Public Health Dynamics Lab at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health. Some people, like small infants and those with weakened immune systems, can't get immunity through a vaccine. "Not vaccinating your kid is like saying, 'I don't want my car to have brakes,'" he said. "Because it's other people that you can hit. It's not just you in your car. It's other people." The Associated Press contributed to this report. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. analysis.brief_en: The U.S. is experiencing a significant measles outbreak with 2,318 confirmed cases across 43 states, surpassing the 2025 record of 2,289 cases. The CDC reports the outbreak has spread to all but seven states, with experts warning the actual number of cases could be much higher, particularly in the Utah-Arizona border region. This surge has put the country at risk of losing its measles elimination status held since 2000. Public health officials emphasize the virus's extreme contagiousness, noting that 9 out of 10 unvaccinated people exposed will become infected. Authorities are urging increased vaccination rates to curb the spread, as the outbreak continues to impact communities nationwide.

news.content: HEALTH Delaware measles cases rise to 4; health officials declare outbreak Isabel Hughes Delaware News Journal July 22, 2026 Updated July 23, 2026, 1:29 p.m. ET The Delaware Division of Public Health has declared a measles outbreak after four people total have now tested positive for the virus. The first positive case was confirmed on July 20. A second came the following day, and two more were confirmed in a July 22 news release. Per the division, a measles outbreak is defined as three or more cases connected by time and location. The definition comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. While details about the cases are limited, DPH said "extensive contact tracing is ongoing" to identify anyone exposed. Who has tested positive for measles in Delaware? The Division of Public Health said all four people who have tested positive are unvaccinated adult men in Kent County. The health department cannot give more information "due to medical privacy restrictions." Who is most at risk during a measles outbreak? People who are unvaccinated, pregnant, immunocompromised or too young to be vaccinated face the highest risk of severe complications, DPH said. The first dose for infants is usually given between 12 and 15 months. Anyone who cannot get the vaccine but who has come into contact with someone suspected to have measles should immediately contact their primary care provider or Delaware's Office of Infectious Disease Epidemiology at (302) 744-4990 for guidance. Are adults who were vaccinated decades ago still protected? If you were born before 1957, you are considered immune. If you were fully vaccinated, you’re also considered immune. If you’re concerned, however, your doctor can order a blood test to check for immunity. Such testing is fairly common. What are measles? Measles is a highly contagious, acute viral illness that begins with early symptoms of fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis (pink eye), lasting two to four days before rash onset. The rash typically occurs three to five days after symptoms begin and usually appears on the face and spreads down the body. Measles can cause severe health complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation and death. The virus is transmitted by direct contact with infectious droplets or by airborne spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The measles virus can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Infected people are contagious from four days before the rash starts through four days after rash development. The incubation period for measles from exposure to fever is usually about 10 days, with a range of seven to 12 days. And from exposure to rash onset is usually about 14 days with a seven to 21-day range. How do you treat measles? There is no specific antiviral cure for the measles . However, if you haven't been previously vaccinated against the measles , you can still be vaccinated to head off the worst symptoms, if you act fast enough. "If people older than six months of age are exposed to measles and are not immune by previous illness or vaccination, they can get a measles vaccine for up to three days after contact with the virus," advised the Mayo Clinic . "After the vaccine you don't need to stay home, also called quarantine." Antibodies can also be given for up to six days after exposure, though they are prioritized for people who cannot get the measles vaccine, such as infants younger than 6 months old, pregnant women, severely immunocompromised people or people who have other medical contraindications to vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. news.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware83° MeaslesMeasles outbreak declared in Delaware; cases also rising in Chester County, Pa.ByBriana Smith Thursday, July 23, 2026 12:13PMMeasles outbreak declared in Delaware; cases also rising in ChescoDOVER, Del. (WPVI) -- Health officials in Delaware and Chester County, Pennsylvania, are urging residents to get vaccinated as measles cases continue to climb across the region.Delaware authorities formally declared a measles outbreak on Wednesday after confirming four cases, all involving unvaccinated adult men in Kent County, Delaware.Dr. Robert Rosenbaum, medical director of the Delaware EMS and Preparedness section, said officials are still working to determine how the patients contracted the airborne virus."Measles is a highly contagious disease. It's why we vaccinate for it," he said.RELATED: Investigation: Big drop in MMR vaccinations at area schoolsRosenbaum added that investigators are conducting "extensive contact tracing for the patients we identified, and we're watching to see if there are any additional cases."Chester County's public health director reported 13 confirmed measles cases and anticipates more.Residents expressed concern about the growing numbers."It's concerning, and I wouldn't be surprised if the numbers go up," said Taylor Williams of Claymont, Del.ALSO SEE: New map shows how to spot the measles risk level in your ZIP codeHealth leaders warn that measles can lead to severe complications and even death. They continue to encourage vaccination to protect vulnerable groups, including infants, older adults and people who are immunocompromised.Rosenbaum emphasized the effectiveness of the vaccine, noting that "the immunity and protection rate with the full vaccination series is well over 97%. If you're vaccinated, you are extremely well protected."He said individuals are considered immune if they were born before 1957, have lab-confirmed immunity, or received two doses of the vaccine between ages 12 and 15 months and again between ages 4 and 6.Some residents voiced support for vaccination efforts."I feel it's the right thing to do, but everybody has their own choice in what they have to do, and they have to live with their decisions," said Joseph Morris of Ocean City, NJ.Rosenbaum said Delaware is working to expand vaccination access through clinics and mobile units.Vaccines are also available at pharmacies and primary care offices. Early symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose and pink eye. They continue to encourage vaccination to protect vulnerable groups, including infants, older adults and people who are immunocompromised.Rosenbaum emphasized the effectiveness of the vaccine, noting that "the immunity and protection rate with the full vaccination series is well over 97%. If you're vaccinated, you are extremely well protected."He said individuals are considered immune if they were born before 1957, have lab-confirmed immunity, or received two doses of the vaccine between ages 12 and 15 months and again between ages 4 and 6.Some residents voiced support for vaccination efforts."I feel it's the right thing to do, but everybody has their own choice in what they have to do, and they have to live with their decisions," said Joseph Morris of Ocean City, NJ.Rosenbaum said Delaware is working to expand vaccination access through clinics and mobile units.Vaccines are also available at pharmacies and primary care offices. Early symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose and pink eye. Health officials advise anyone experiencing these signs to seek immediate care.Report a correction or typoCopyright © 2026 WPVI-TV. news.content: 24/7 LiveHoustonSouthwestSoutheastNorthwestNortheast93° Measles4 cases of measles confirmed in Montgomery County, health officials sayWednesday, July 22, 2026 9:45PMMeasles, also known as rubeola, is a highly contagious viral infection that causes fever and a full-body rash. It can lead to potentially fatal complications like dehydration, respiratory infections and a brain-swelling infection called encephalitis.Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Cynthia Goldsmith, AP Photo/Damian DovarganesMONTGOMERY COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- The Montgomery County Public Health Department has confirmed four cases of measles.Officials say the cases in the county involve four family members who were exposed to another confirmed case involving someone who traveled from out of state.On Tuesday afternoon, health officials announced the fourth case involves a woman in the same family who is between 20 and 30 years old, and is now hospitalized.The video above is from a previous report.According to the health department, none of the people who were infected had been vaccinated. Health officials said measles is highly contagious and can be life-threatening, especially in children younger than 5 years old.Officials said the virus spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.Some of the symptoms include a fever over 101 F, cough, runny nose, red, watery eyes, and a rash, and can appear seven to 14 days after contact with the virus.Report a correction or typoCopyright © 2026 KTRK-TV. Health officials said measles is highly contagious and can be life-threatening, especially in children younger than 5 years old.Officials said the virus spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.Some of the symptoms include a fever over 101 F, cough, runny nose, red, watery eyes, and a rash, and can appear seven to 14 days after contact with the virus.Report a correction or typoCopyright © 2026 KTRK-TV. analysis.brief_en: Montgomery County, Texas health officials have confirmed four cases of measles, involving four family members exposed to a traveler from out of state. One woman, aged 20-30, is hospitalized. None of the infected individuals had been vaccinated. Measles, a highly contagious viral infection, can lead to severe complications including encephalitis, particularly in young children. The virus spreads through airborne transmission, causing symptoms like fever, cough, runny nose, and rash. Health authorities are urging vaccination to prevent further spread and are conducting contact tracing to contain the outbreak.

The report highlights that this cooperation issue is complicating efforts to control the spread of the virus in the state. This outbreak occurs as Pennsylvania grapples with a separate, larger measles outbreak that has seen 120 cases since April, with 72 reported in Lancaster County alone. The MMR vaccine remains highly effective at preventing the disease, with a 97% efficacy rate.

Health officials are actively conducting contact tracing to identify potential exposures. This outbreak occurs as Pennsylvania grapples with a separate, larger measles outbreak that has seen 120 cases since April, with 72 reported in Lancaster County alone. Measles, known for its high contagiousness, can lead to severe complications including pneumonia and brain inflammation. The MMR vaccine remains highly effective at preventing the disease, with a 97% efficacy rate.

analysis.brief_en: The United States has experienced a significant measles outbreak, with cases reaching a 35-year high for the second consecutive year. This resurgence marks a stark contrast to the disease's elimination status in the country since 2000. Public health experts are concerned about the implications for community immunity and the potential for further spread. The outbreak underscores ongoing challenges in maintaining vaccination coverage and addressing vaccine hesitancy. Health authorities are likely monitoring the situation closely, though specific response measures have not been detailed in the available information.

news.title_zh: 美国 麻疹 病例创 35 年来新高,连续第二年破纪录 - CNN
news.source_body_en: The United States has experienced a significant measles outbreak, with cases reaching a 35-year high for the second consecutive year. This resurgence marks a stark contrast to the disease's elimination status in the country since 2000. Public health experts are concerned about the implications for community immunity and the potential for further spread. The outbreak underscores ongoing challenges in maintaining vaccination coverage and addressing vaccine hesitancy. Health authorities are likely monitoring the situation closely, though specific response measures have not been detailed in the available information.

supplementary_news.content_title: Oral drug candidate blocks transmission of measles-like disease in ferrets
supplementary_news.content: A new oral antiviral drug candidate administered either before or after direct contact or airborne exposure to canine distemper virus, which causes measles-like disease in ferrets, blocks transmission of the virus and reduces clinical symptoms, according to a study published in the journal Nature Microbiology by researchers in the Center for Translational Antiviral Research (CTAR) at Georgia State University. The study explored whether prophylactic (shortly before or after exposure) administration of the recently developed clinical candidate GHP-88310 (described in Science Advances), a broad-spectrum inhibitor of the viral polymerase, prevents virus transmission through close contact or through the air. The results demonstrate that GHP-88310 efficiently blocks both forms of viral spread. In addition, the study showed that treatment of infected animals shortened the time period in which infected animals could transmit the virus. Silencing measles outbreaks quickly is essential to reestablish control over the virus. This study follows our recent development of the drug candidate GHP-88310. It demonstrates that the drug is suitable to augment traditional ring vaccination against measles." Richard Plemper, senior author, a Regents' Professor and director of the CTAR Since 2025, measles has reemerged in the United States with thousands of cases across multiple states, hundreds of hospitalizations and three confirmed deaths. Large outbreaks in Canada and Mexico with multiple deaths have challenged the measles elimination status of North America. "We were very excited to see that GHP-88310 given by mouth completely prevented airborne transmission in our ferret model of measles," said first author Carolin Lieber, a senior postdoctoral fellow in the Plemper lab. "This finding is unprecedented for a viral polymerase inhibitor and demonstrates the extraordinary antiviral potency of this drug." To explore relevant conditions of viral transmission, the researchers developed a system that allowed them to pair infected and uninfected animals in direct physical contact or shared airspace, each under controlled environmental parameters. "We designed the study to recapitulate viral spread between people with direct contact, for instance in a household, and between more distant social contacts, for example in classrooms or other indoor settings that bring people into proximity without direct interaction," said Plemper. "In addition to this prophylactic benefit, GHP-88310 used therapeutically shortened the duration of disease in our model. If equally applicable to human hosts, it may shorten the severe social and economic burden of prolonged quarantine of patients and further aid outbreak management." The investigators are now readying GHP-88310 for formal clinical testing. Additional authors of the study include Josef Wolf, Claire Ruckel and Lauren Harrison of the Center for Translational Antiviral Research in the Institute for Biomedical Sciences at Georgia State. The study was funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Source: Journal reference: Lieber, C. M., et al . (2026). Antiviral GHP-88310 blocks contact-mediated and airborne transmission in a ferret model of measles-like disease. Nature Microbiology. DOI: 10.1038/s41564-026-02419-y. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-026-02419-y
